title: CuSearch: Curriculum Rollout Sampling via Search Depth for Agentic RAG

paper.title: CuSearch: Curriculum Rollout Sampling via Search Depth for Agentic RAG
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards ( RLVR ) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training agentic retrieval-augmented generation ( RAG ) systems from outcome-only supervision.
Most existing methods optimize policies from uniformly sampled rollouts, implicitly treating all trajectories as equally informative.
However, trajectories differ substantially in search depth and are therefore not equally informative: deeper-search trajectories contain more retrieval decision points and provide denser direct supervision for the retrieval sub-policy.
Moreover, this heterogeneity grows over training as the within-batch depth distribution shifts toward higher values, yet uniform rollout sampling remains blind to this shift.
To address this, we propose CuSearch , a curriculum rollout sampling framework built on Search-Depth Greedy Allocation (SDGA) , a batch-level operator that reallocates a fixed update budget toward deeper-search trajectories. SDGA-Auto always targets the deepest available trajectories in the current batch, yielding an implicit training-aligned curriculum as the depth distribution shifts upward. SDGA-Phase explicitly advances the curriculum threshold as deeper trajectories become sufficiently abundant.
Experiments across model types and retrieval frameworks show that CuSearch consistently improves performance, achieving up to 11.8 exact-match points over standard GRPO on ZeroSearch .
These results establish per-trajectory search depth as a reliable, annotation-free proxy for retrieval supervision density in RLVR-based agentic RAG training.
The code is available at https://github.com/MrToser/CuSearch .

The code is available at https://github.com/MrToser/CuSearch . 1 Introduction Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for training large language models (LLMs) from outcome-only supervision ( Lee et al., 2009 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . This paradigm has been extended to agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , where models learn to decide when to retrieve and what to query during reasoning. For knowledge-intensive tasks, model parameters alone cannot cover all relevant facts, making the ability to actively retrieve external information at inference time essential. Earlier systems relied on heuristic triggers ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Trivedi et al., 2023 ) or supervised fine-tuning on expert trajectories ( Asai et al., 2023 ; Nakano et al., 2021 ) . Contemporary RLVR-based methods ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) now optimize retrieval policies solely through final answer rewards, bypassing manual design or expert traces. Despite this potential, existing methods optimize policies from uniformly sampled rollouts ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) , implicitly treating all trajectories as equally informative. For the same prompt, trajectories can vary substantially in search depth, defined as the number of valid search steps they issue. Search depth provides a simple structural indicator of how many retrieval decision points a trajectory exposes and thus serves as a practical proxy for how much direct supervision it provides for the retrieval sub-policy. Treating these unequally informative trajectories as equivalent allocates the update budget indiscriminately. This dilutes the influence of deeper-search trajectories and assigns optimization budget to rollouts with minimal retrieval learning value. Existing work on non-uniform sample usage has largely operated at the prompt level, filtering or reallocating the training budget based on prompt-level signals such as reward variance, estimated difficulty, or expected policy improvement ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) . By aggregating statistics across rollouts for the same prompt, these approaches discard within-batch variation in individual trajectory search behavior. Process-based supervision ( Lightman et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ) provides denser intermediate feedback but requires additional annotation or auxiliary models. None of these approaches exploit search depth, an annotation-free and trajectory-intrinsic structural signal for retrieval supervision density. Over the course of training, answer-correctness reward reinforces retrieval behavior, and per-trajectory search depth increases monotonically. As shown in Figure 1 , the within-batch depth distribution shifts toward larger values as RLVR progresses, deepening the informativeness gap across trajectories and making the misallocation of the update budget increasingly consequential. This temporal shift motivates a trajectory-level curriculum that concentrates the update budget on the deepest available trajectories within each batch and naturally advances as the depth distribution shifts upward. Figure 1: (a) Average search count per trajectory increases over training under answer-correctness reward alone. (b) The within-batch depth distribution shifts toward higher values as training advances. Motivated by these observations, we propose CuSearch , a curriculum rollout sampling framework for agentic RAG. At the core of CuSearch is Search-Depth Greedy Allocation (SDGA) , a batch-level operator that selects K K trajectories from a larger pool of N ⋅ G N\cdot G rollouts, restricting reward normalization, advantage estimation, and gradient updates to this subset. Crucially, SDGA selects by search depth rather than by reward. It prefers trajectories that expose more retrieval decision points, even when final rewards are similar. We instantiate SDGA in two variants. SDGA-Auto always targets the deepest available trajectories in the current batch, yielding an implicit training-aligned curriculum as the depth distribution shifts upward. SDGA-Phase makes this curriculum explicit, advancing a phase threshold irreversibly toward deeper trajectories as they become sufficiently abundant in the rollout pool. Experiments across model types and retrieval frameworks show that CuSearch consistently improves final performance under comparable rollout budgets. Gains reach up to 11.8 exact-match points over standard GRPO on ZeroSearch, with substantial margins over prompt-level adaptive methods such as DAPO and AR3PO. Our contributions are: 1. We identify and empirically characterize a training dynamic in agentic RAG: under answer-correctness reward alone, per-trajectory search depth increases over training, increasing the heterogeneity in retrieval supervision density across trajectories. 2. We propose CuSearch , a framework built on the SDGA operator, with two instantiations. SDGA-Auto is a stateless greedy variant that always targets the deepest available trajectories, yielding an implicit training-aligned curriculum as the depth distribution shifts upward. SDGA-Phase is an explicit phase-adaptive variant that advances the curriculum threshold as deeper trajectories become sufficiently abundant. Both reallocate a fixed update budget toward deeper-search trajectories without additional annotation or auxiliary models. 3. We demonstrate consistent gains across two model families, two retrieval frameworks, and seven benchmarks. We further identify two factors governing gain magnitude: search depth growth during training as the primary driver, and retrieval-environment stochasticity as a secondary amplifier. 2 Related Work 2.1 Agentic RAG Training with Reinforcement Learning Early RAG methods retrieve a fixed set of documents and condition generation on them statically ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) . Subsequent agentic retrieval methods interleave reasoning and retrieval over multiple steps, enabling models to gather evidence adaptively during inference ( Singh et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2022 ) . Representative examples include ReAct ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , FLARE ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , and IRCoT ( Trivedi et al., 2023 ) . While these approaches improve retrieval–reasoning coordination, their interaction protocols are typically predefined or rely on heuristic retrieval control, rather than being optimized end-to-end from answer rewards. Recent work extends RLVR to agentic RAG and directly optimizes retrieval behavior from outcome-only supervision. Search-R1 ( Jin et al., 2025 ) , R1-Searcher ( Song et al., 2025 ) , ZeroSearch ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , ReZero ( Dao and Le, 2025 ) , RAG-Gym ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) , and ReasonRAG ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) study RL-based retrieval optimization through different training recipes, retrieval environments, and reward formulations. Our work is complementary to this line of research. Rather than introducing a new retrieval environment or auxiliary reward signal, we study how a fixed update budget should be allocated across trajectories during training. Specifically, we use per-trajectory search depth as an annotation-free structural proxy for trajectory informativeness, and prioritize trajectories that expose denser supervision signal for the retrieval sub-policy. 2.2 Curriculum and Adaptive Sampling in RL Curriculum learning improves optimization by prioritizing training samples with greater learning value ( Bengio et al., 2009 ) . Prioritized experience replay ( Schaul et al., 2015 ) selects transitions by temporal-difference error, and DART-Math ( Tong et al., 2024 ) applies difficulty-aware rejection sampling in supervised fine-tuning. Recent RLVR methods extend this principle to prompt-level allocation ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025b ) , filtering or reallocating gradient budget based on prompt-level signals such as reward variance, estimated difficulty, or expected policy improvement ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Le et al., 2025 ; Bae et al., 2026 ) . However, these approaches primarily focus on prompt-level allocation, loss-based prioritization, or offline data construction. None of them exploit the per-trajectory structural signal that governs retrieval informativeness within a training batch. Complementary work studies rollout structure: Depth-Breadth Synergy ( Yang et al., 2025 ) balances reasoning depth and diversity, InfoFlow ( Obregon et al., 2019 ) optimizes reward density, and process supervision ( Lightman et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ) provides step-level annotations. CuSearch operates at the trajectory level rather than the prompt level, and uses search depth as a structural signal rather than a reward-derived one. Prompt-level methods decide which prompts enter training, while CuSearch decides, from the rollouts already generated, which trajectories most directly cover the retrieval decision space. These two operations are orthogonal, and the gains of CuSearch over prompt-level baselines under matched compute confirm that trajectory-level structural selection addresses a distinct dimension of the training allocation problem.
